title: What does go
hookLine: the Name and good deeds go along (Sukhmani 19)

cards: At the airport check-in desk there's a scale, and a number on a sign: fifty pounds. Anything over that costs you, or stays home.

So people kneel on the floor of the terminal, unzipping suitcases, pulling out the extra shoes, the heavy book, the jar of pickle from an aunt. It's a strange little moment of truth. What actually matters enough to carry?
Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi has its own scale, and its own short list.

teach.h: THE SALOK: NOTHING ELSE GOES ALONG.
teach.b: Go back two days, to the salok that opens the nineteenth ashtpadi. Its first line said nothing goes along without devotion.
Its second line already holds today's answer: earn the Name of the Lord, says Nanak; this is the wealth worth having.
The verb is kamaavanaa, to earn: the ordinary Punjabi word for earning a living, a day's wages. So the Name isn't pictured as a lottery ticket.

It's earned the way bread is earned, by showing up, again and again, over years. And it's the one kind of savings the scale at the end can't weigh out. Then there's a second thing that travels: what you've done.

teach.h: YOUR DEEDS BRING YOU NEAR OR FAR.
teach.b: Sikhs hear this in the closing salok of Japji, the morning prayer: by their own deeds, some come near and some go far.
Guru Nanak's teaching is often summed up in three short phrases: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share what you have. Two of the three are about how you treat other people.
Read that way, the soul doesn't carry a trophy shelf or a bank balance.
It carries a character: what it became through the remembering and the giving.
Kindness done isn't a thing you own; it's something you've turned into. That's why it fits in the bag. And there's a quiet comfort in that.
You can't take the house or the title. But the part of you that learned to be generous? Read with Japji's closing line, that's the part that comes along.

how: Sikhs reciting the nineteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib hear that only the Name, earned through practice, goes along at the end; many sum up Guru Nanak's way as remembering the Name, honest work and sharing.

o: by rank: the family you're born into
by deeds: what we do brings us near or far
by luck, the way a lottery is won

games.q: what does go — tap the pairs.
p: to earn, like a day's wages
by our deeds, near or far

s: the salok pictures the Name as something won by luck
it uses kamaavanaa, to earn: the Name is earned like a living.
two of Guru Nanak's three short phrases are about how we treat others
earning honestly and sharing both turn outward.
Sikh teaching pictures the soul carrying its bank balance
it carries what it became through remembering and giving.

games.q: the scale at the end weighs everything. what does the nineteenth ashtpadi say makes it through?
o: the house, if it's paid off.
the Name you earned, and what your deeds made of you.
games.why: the salok says all the rest is ash; the earned Name is the wealth worth having, and Japji adds that deeds bring us near or far.

practice: Bring to mind one person who could use something real from you, something that will still be true next month: an hour, a skill, a long-overdue apology, a regular phone call.
Picture yourself doing it, all the way through, and see the first small step. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Karmee, by deeds: in Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi only the earned Name goes along, and in Sikh teaching karmee, our deeds, bring us near or far.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: karmee, by deeds, from Japji's closing salok: by their own deeds, some come near and some go far.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness travels. You carry what you became, not what you owned. See you tomorrow.
